passage: Lata, you want to know how I learned to lose an argument? Sit down, I'm Keerthana and I will tell you. I was twenty, in the college debate group, and I was sure our hostel needed a later gate time. I stood up with my figures, very pleased with myself. Dhruv, at the back, said, "Your survey only asked people on your own floor." My face went hot. I wanted to say that the floor was enough. But he was right, and I knew it, so I said, "You are right about that. Give me a week." I walked through every block with my sheet. The new numbers were messier and the proposal was better. The warden read every page, and Dhruv helped me count the sheets, arguing with me about the results all the way to the canteen.

qa.q: Whose survey only asked people on one floor, and who pointed this out?
qa.a: Keerthana's survey only asked people on Keerthana's own floor, and Dhruv pointed it out from the back of the debate group.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when Dhruv spoke, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Keerthana felt stung and embarrassed. Their face went hot and they wanted to say the floor was enough, before choosing to admit the point.

qa.q: What did Keerthana decide to do after Dhruv's remark, and how did it change the proposal?
qa.a: Keerthana admitted Dhruv was right, asked for a week and went to every block. The numbers were messier but the proposal was better and the warden read every page.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have felt when Keerthana said "You are right about that"?
qa.a: Dhruv probably felt heard and respected, since Keerthana did not defend the weak survey and later even counted sheets together with Dhruv. 🙂

grounding: A young adult concedes a good counter-argument, adjusts the plan and gains credibility, told by the elder as a memory.

passage:
Twelve minutes before their final viva, Samir and Vandana were still arguing over the slide order in the corridor outside the seminar room.
"Numbers first," Samir said. "The examiners like proof."
"If they do not care about the problem, the numbers are just noise," Vandana said, holding the laptop against a hip. "Open with the woman from the survey who walked four kilometres for water."
Samir looked at the clock, then at the slides. His jaw tightened and loosened. "Fair point. Story first. But the biggest number goes in your opening sentence."
"Deal."
They dragged three slides, fixed one title, and walked in with the projector already warm.

qa.q: How many minutes were left before the viva when the argument began?
qa.a: Twelve minutes were left before their final viva.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when the jaw tightened and then loosened?
qa.a: Samir felt pressured and a little reluctant, since the clock was running and the plan was theirs. Then Samir let go of the argument and accepted the better order.

qa.q: What did Samir change after saying "Fair point", and what stayed the same?
qa.a: Samir agreed to put the story first, and kept the proof by asking that the biggest number go in Vandana's opening sentence.

qa.q: What would it have been like for Vandana if Samir had kept insisting on numbers first?
qa.a: Vandana would probably have felt unheard and anxious, with the clock running and the argument still going as they walked in. Samir's quick concession left them free to prepare.

grounding: Under time pressure, a young adult says a fair point was made and changes the slide order to suit the better argument.

passage:
The canteen at the Pune college was nearly empty when Omkar and Swati sat down to prepare for Friday's inter-college debate. Their motion was whether the city should ban private cars from the old market lanes on weekends.
"Shopkeepers will lose customers," Omkar said, tapping his notebook. "Nobody carries heavy bags from a bus stop."
Swati slid her phone across. "The trader association did a count last year. On the two trial Sundays, footfall went up, because families could walk without dodging scooters."
Omkar read it twice. He frowned, then laughed at himself. "That's a fair point. Okay, so my real worry is deliveries, not customers."
He crossed out his first line and wrote: allow early-morning delivery vans.
On Friday, when the other team pushed back, Swati turned to him first. "Omkar, you take the delivery question. They'll believe you."

qa.q: What did the trader association count show about the two trial Sundays?
qa.a: Footfall went up on the two trial Sundays, because families could walk without dodging scooters.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when he read Swati's figures, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was briefly thrown and a little embarrassed, shown by his frown, but then relaxed enough to laugh at himself and accept it rather than defend his first claim.

qa.q: What small habit could help Omkar keep arguing this way in future debates?
qa.a: Before digging in, he could ask himself what his real worry is, as he did with deliveries, so he can drop a weak claim and keep the strong one.

qa.q: How does Swati see Omkar after he changes his position?
qa.a: She trusts his judgement more, which is why she hands him the delivery question on Friday and says the other team will believe him.

grounding: A young adult says that was a fair point, adjusts the argument, and gains a teammate's trust as a result.

passage:
"We can't cite this," Nandini said, turning her laptop towards Sarika in the library's group room. "Look, the blog doesn't name a single study."
"It's the clearest explanation of groundwater loss I've found," Sarika said. "And we have to submit by six."
"Clear isn't the same as true. Who wrote it?"
"Someone who runs a water blog. Nandini, it matches what Professor Iyer said."
"Then let's cite what Professor Iyer said. Or the report she mentioned."
Sarika opened her mouth, closed it, and scrolled up. No author page. No references.
"Fine. You're right, and I was just tired. If I'd submitted this and she asked me where the numbers came from, I'd have nothing."
"I'm not trying to win," Nandini said.
"I know. That's why it's easy to say you're right." Sarika opened the university library search. "Give me twenty minutes to find the report."

qa.q: Where were Sarika and Nandini working?
qa.a: They were in the library's group room.

qa.q: Why did Sarika resist Nandini's point at first?
qa.a: Sarika was tired and felt pressured by the six o'clock deadline, and the blog was the clearest explanation found so far, so dropping it felt frustrating.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Sarika checked for an author page and references, admitted Nandini was right, and went to find the report; testing the source rather than defending it protected their project.

qa.q: What is it like for Nandini when Sarika concedes?
qa.a: Nandini feels relieved and respected, since the aim was a sound project, not a win, and Sarika's quick agreement shows they are on the same side.

grounding: A student concedes a teammate's better argument about a source and changes course, showing the goal is getting it right.

passage:
I'm Himani, and I still remember the eco club meeting in second year when I was sure I had the perfect plan. I wanted our campus cleanup on Sunday mornings, when the paths are empty and we could work fast.
Mohit listened, rubbed his chin, then said quietly, "Half the volunteers are day scholars. They'd need two buses each way on a Sunday. You'd get the hostel crowd and nobody else."
My face went hot. I had built a whole poster already. For a second I wanted to say the day scholars should just make the effort.
Instead I heard myself say, "That's fair. I planned it around my own timetable."
We moved it to Wednesday lunch. Forty people came instead of the usual twelve. What surprised me more was later: when I proposed the compost pit, nobody argued. Mohit said, "If Himani checked it, it's fine."

qa.q: When did Himani first want the campus cleanup to happen?
qa.a: Himani wanted it on Sunday mornings, when the paths are empty.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when Mohit raised the bus problem?
qa.a: Himani felt embarrassed and defensive, shown by the hot face and the urge to say the day scholars should just make the effort, especially after already making a poster.

qa.q: What could Himani carry forward from this meeting?
qa.a: Before settling a plan, Himani could ask who else it affects, and keep saying so openly when someone points out a gap.

qa.q: How does Mohit see Himani after the meeting?
qa.a: Mohit sees Himani as someone who checks ideas honestly, which is why he backs the compost pit without arguing.

grounding: A young adult concedes a fair point about volunteers' travel, adjusts the plan, and gains credibility for later proposals.

passage: Coach's log, debate society practice, Wednesday. Motion: the college canteen should go fully cashless. Aparna argued for, Madhuri against. Aparna opened strongly with queue times and lost change. Madhuri answered with one example: the canteen's cleaning staff, and two hostel students she knew who have no bank card and pay in coins. Aparna started to rebut, stopped, and said, "Okay, that's fair. I hadn't counted them." She rewrote her closing on the spot: cashless by default, with one cash counter kept open. Two first-years in the audience looked surprised; afterwards they told me they had thought conceding meant losing. When we scored, Aparna got the highest credibility mark of the evening, and Madhuri said she would trust Aparna's numbers more next time because of it. Next week I am adding a round where each speaker must name one point from the other side that they accept.

qa.q: What was the motion at Wednesday's practice?
qa.a: The college canteen should go fully cashless.

qa.q: What might Aparna have felt when she stopped in the middle of her rebuttal?
qa.a: She probably felt a flash of uncertainty and then openness, seeing that Madhuri's example was real and that her own plan had left people out.

qa.q: What small practice is the coach adding, and why might it help?
qa.a: A round where each speaker names one point from the other side they accept; it makes conceding feel normal instead of like losing.

qa.q: How did Aparna's concession look to Madhuri?
qa.a: Madhuri came to trust Aparna's numbers more, because the concession showed Aparna cared more about getting it right than about winning.

grounding: Shows a young adult accepting an opponent's good point and adjusting her position, and gaining credibility for it.
